summary: Solstice Health performed a technical security review focused on encryption controls. Redwood explained encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integrations (AWS/GCP/Azure), BYOK flows, HSM options, key rotation, key access logs and evidence for auditors. Customer requested detailed BYOK integration steps, sample KMS policies, SOC2 artifact sharing, and to schedule a POC network checklist call.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hi everyone, thanks for joining. we’re going to cover encryption controls and key management, feel free to interrupt.
[00:10] Aisha Rahman: thanks maya. quick ask up front — we’re regulated, so primary concerns are BYOK, HSM support, and auditability for key access for our SOC 2 auditor.
[00:22] Maya Chen: absolutely. ethan and ravi from our security/solutions team are here to dig in.
[00:26] Ethan Park: hey all. quick agenda: encryption in transit, encryption at rest, KMS integrations across clouds, BYOK flows, HSM options, rotation and audit logs, and then q&a.
[00:36] Daniel Ortiz: sounds good. we’re on aws primarily but have some gcp for analytics. we need to understand how Redwood’s managed service can plug into our existing KMS and HSMs.
[00:48] Priya Kapoor: and data residency — our PHI data must stay in us-east-1. we need confirmation that keys and ciphertext residency maps to that.
[00:56] Ethan Park: got it. starting high level — all traffic to Redwood endpoints is TLS 1.2/1.3, mutual TLS supported for dedicated/private deployments, so encryption in transit is standard. for encryption at rest, we use envelope encryption: model request payloads are encrypted with a data encryption key (DEK), which itself is wrapped by a customer master key (CMK) managed in a KMS.
[01:20] Aisha Rahman: when you say "managed in KMS", do you mean Redwood’s keys or the customer's keys?
[01:25] Ravi Patel: we support both. by default Redwood can manage the CMK; for BYOK you supply your own CMK in your cloud KMS — aws kms, gcp cloud kms, or azure key vault — and we never persist the plaintext CMK.
[01:38] Tom James: do you support HSM-backed keys? our security team requires HSM roots for production PHI.
[01:44] Ethan Park: yes. we support HSM-backed CMKs via cloud HSM (aws cloudhsm->aws kms with HSM key material) and also accept customer-managed HSMs for private deployments. for hosted customers we accept CMEK/HSM keys in the supported cloud KMS. for private/on-prem customers we can integrate with on-prem HSMs using PKCS#11 or vendor APIs.
[02:05] Priya Kapoor: can you walk through the BYOK flow? specifically, where do we upload key material, and how is access to the key restricted?
[02:13] Ravi Patel: sure. typical aws BYOK flow: you create a CMK in your AWS account (optionally backed by CloudHSM), set a key policy that allows Redwood service principal to use the key for encrypt/decrypt operations. Redwood only gets an encrypted token that lets our data plane call AWS KMS in your account; we never take custody of raw key material. all requests to KMS are logged in your cloud account's KMS audit logs (cloudtrail).
[02:35] Aisha Rahman: i’m concerned about the necessity to give Redwood use permissions — auditors want proof Redwood cannot export keys or decrypt outside our control.
[02:45] Ethan Park: understood. the pattern we recommend is to limit Redwood to "kms:Encrypt","kms:Decrypt" and possibly "kms:GenerateDataKey" only, with a condition that restricts usage to specific endpoints and the Redwood service principal. we can provide example IAM policies. the key policy sits in your account so you control key grants, and you can revoke them at any time.
[03:05] Daniel Ortiz: that’s helpful. what about key rotation? our standard is rotate root keys annually and DEKs more frequently. how does Redwood handle rotate without downtime?
[03:15] Ravi Patel: envelope encryption helps — DEKs are generated per object or per time window via GenerateDataKey; when you rotate the CMK, new DEKs are wrapped with the new CMK. Redwood can support rotation with a staged rollover: old CMK kept for decrypting existing ciphertext, new CMK used for new encrypt operations. we keep metadata so we know which CMK wrapped which payload.
[03:36] Priya Kapoor: the metadata — where is it stored and is it tamper-evident for auditor requests?
[03:41] Ethan Park: metadata is stored in our control plane metadata store with audit logs. for dedicated/private setups the metadata stays in your VPC/tenant isolation. all key usage events are also recorded in both our access logs and we rely on your cloud provider's KMS logs. we can provide export of these logs for auditors.
[03:58] Aisha Rahman: speaking of logs, we need tamper-proof audit trails — do you support write-once logs or integration with our SIEM?
[04:06] Ravi Patel: yes — we push syslogs and structured audit events to customer destinations for Dedicated and Private: you can push to CloudWatch, Stackdriver, or your syslog/SIEM via secure forwarders. logs include request id, timestamp, operation (Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey), caller identity, and which CMK was used. we also support signed log export for longer-term retention.
[04:30] Tom James: for hosted customers, how do you prevent cross-tenant access?
[04:34] Ethan Park: multi-tenancy is handled at several layers: network isolation, tenant-scoped metadata, and per-tenant KMS usage. for BYOK hosted we'll call your KMS in your cloud account, so the key policy prevents cross-tenant use. data plane isolation and encryption keys are tenant-bound.
[04:50] Daniel Ortiz: what about private control plane vs data plane? our compliance team insists private control plane so tokens and metadata don't leave our VPC.
[04:58] Ravi Patel: we offer a private deployment option where the control plane endpoints are in your VPC; the data plane can be colocated. tokens and metadata remain in your environment; Redwood personnel access is via customer-managed Bastion with RBAC and SSO integration.
[05:12] Priya Kapoor: SSO/RBAC — do you integrate with our identity provider for key access approvals or just for admin console?
[05:18] Ethan Park: SSO via SAML/OIDC for console/console admin; for key operations, authorization is via the cloud KMS policies and your IAM. we also support attribute-based access controls for role separation in Dedicated/Private setups.
[05:32] Aisha Rahman: auditors ask for evidence of separation of duties. how would you demonstrate Redwood engineers don’t have access to plaintext keys or decrypted PHI?
[05:40] Maya Chen: short answer: they don’t. long answer: with BYOK and HSM we never see key material; access to decryption paths requires explicit KMS grants from your account. for logs, we can provide trails showing requests, and for private deployments engineers only get access via customer-managed bastion and recorded sessions.
[05:57] Daniel Ortiz: any limitations with ephemeral caching or KV cache in memory that could expose plaintext?
[06:03] Ethan Park: good question. our runtime uses in-memory DEKs only scoped to the request lifecycle, and we zero memory after use. for long-running caches we store only ciphertext. for dedicated/private we can disable caching if required.
[06:20] Priya Kapoor: can you support HSM-backed import of keys so root never leaves our HSM?
[06:25] Ravi Patel: yes — for on-prem HSMs using PKCS#11 you can generate keys in your HSM and provide a wrapped key token or allow Redwood to call your HSM via network boundary. for cloud HSM we recommend AWS CloudHSM or Google Cloud HSM where key material remains in HSM.
[06:40] Tom James: what about legal hold and key escrow — do you offer escrow or do we have to manage that?
[06:46] Ethan Park: we do not hold escrow for BYOK scenarios; key escrow is up to the customer. if you want Redwood-managed keys we can offer a managed key escrow under contract, but for compliance it's typical customers want to keep control.
[07:00] Aisha Rahman: auditors often want to see documented key rotation procedures and evidence that old keys are retired. can you provide sample artifacts?
[07:07] Maya Chen: yes — we'll share a rotation playbook and sample rotation logs.
[07:11] Daniel Ortiz: do you have latency implications when calling customer KMS in our account? we’re sensitive to token latency.
[07:17] Ravi Patel: there's a small overhead on GenerateDataKey calls — typically tens to low hundreds of milliseconds depending on region and KMS. we mitigate with local DEK caching (re-wrapping) and batching where allowed. for low-latency SLOs we recommend dedicated/private deployments in same region as your KMS and colocated HSMs.
[07:35] Priya Kapoor: what about data residency? if ciphertext is stored in Redwood’s storage, can we ensure it stays in us-east-1?
[07:41] Ethan Park: yes — in Dedicated/Private you can control region; for hosted we offer region selection and can commit to resident storage in supported regions. we can include region constraints in contract for PHI workloads.
[07:55] Aisha Rahman: are there any known gaps in your current offering compared to SOC2 requirements?
[07:59] Maya Chen: we are SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified for our hosted, and we have documented controls for encryption, access control, logging, and incident response. for private deployments some controls map to customer responsibilities — we will provide RACI.
[08:13] Tom James: show me the artifacts — SOC 2 report, ISO cert, pen test summary.
[08:17] Maya Chen: will share post-call.
[08:20] Priya Kapoor: can you support FIPS 140-2 validated crypto modules?
[08:24] Ethan Park: we rely on cloud provider crypto; if you need FIPS validated modules, cloud KMS can be configured for FIPS endpoints or you can use FIPS HSMs in private deployments. we can provide guidance for the configuration.
[08:38] Daniel Ortiz: any difference for embeddings or logs that might include PII — do you treat them differently?
[08:44] Ravi Patel: same encryption model applies. we recommend tokenization or redaction pre-ingest for high-sensitivity PII; otherwise payloads are encrypted with DEKs and wrapped by your CMK.
[08:58] Aisha Rahman: on auditors' evidence — you mentioned cloudtrail and your access logs. can you export signed copies for audits?
[09:05] Ethan Park: yes, we can provide signed exports of structured events and we recommend you also pull KMS-level logs from your account cloudtrail for independent verification.
[09:17] Maya Chen: ok, looks like we have a few concrete asks — we’ll share SOC/ISO artifacts, BYOK step-by-step, example IAM/key policies, rotation playbook, and a sample log export.
[09:27] Priya Kapoor: and a network checklist for private POC.
[09:30] Maya Chen: yes.
[09:32] Tom James: are there any blockers we should be aware of for a November pilot?
[09:36] Ethan Park: from a product side no blockers; main items are KMS keys to set up, policy grants, and networking for private POC. those are straightforward.
[09:45] Daniel Ortiz: ok. last thing — can we get a short technical runbook for our auditors describing the flow from request -> DEK -> KMS -> storage?
[09:53] Ravi Patel: yes, we'll produce a one-pager runbook and a deeper architecture doc.
[09:58] Maya Chen: great. thanks everyone. quick recap and next steps...
[10:03] Maya Chen: recap: maya to send SOC2/ISO artifacts, ethan to prepare BYOK/HSM guide and IAM policy examples, ravi to draft rotation playbook and runbook, priya will circulate auditor evidence list and we’ll schedule the POC network checklist call.
[10:20] Aisha Rahman: thanks. that addresses our main concerns.
[10:23] Tom James: thanks team — we’ll review and reach out.
[10:26] Maya Chen: i'll follow up with the docs and calendar invite. bye all.
